newsitem.title: USA: France can meet Maastricht budget deficit goal - IMF.
newsitem.headline: France can meet Maastricht budget deficit goal - IMF.

text.p: A senior IMF official said on Monday that it was "perfectly feasible" that France will succeed in reducing its government budget deficit next year to 3 percent of gross domestic product.

But the International Monetary Fund official, who declined to be identified, told reporters that that depends on Paris carrying out the budget plans it unveiled last week and French economic growth picking up next year as expected.

"If the present indications we have on the perspective for 1997 are confirmed -- namely a rate of growth of about 2.5 percent -- it is perfectly feasible, provided the government steadily implements the budget program," he said.
The 3 percent threshold for the budget deficit was set out in the Maastricht treaty for participation by European countries in European Monetary Union (EMU), which is due to be launched in 1999.

Briefing reporters ahead of the start of the IMF/World Bank annual meeting here later this week, the senior official also welcomed Italy's determination to reduce its budget deficit in the face of slowing economic growth.
Italy is shooting to reduce its budget deficit to 3 percent of GDP in 1998 -- one year after the target date set out in Maastricht for participation in the launch of EMU.
The senior IMF official said Italy's ability to reach its 1998 objective will depend crucially on the course of the economy in the coming years.

"If you have the desirable strengthening of the economy, not only in Italy but in the whole of Western Europe, then the conditions could allow for the extra effort that will be needed for (Italy to achieve its goal)," he said.
To succeed in its drive to cut the deficit, Italy though, will have to tackle such "sensitive" areas as health care, pension reform and government workers' wages, the senior IMF official said.

He also made clear that France needs to take tough decisions to rein in government spending. "Maastricht or not, they have a major problem and indispensable action to take if they want to recover sustainable (economic) growth," he said.
He warned Paris that it would face "much higher" interest rates on its government debt if it abandoned its fiscal discipline.
